blogs.title: From 16‑Bit to 1.58‑Bit: How BitNet b1.58 Keeps Language Models Sharp
blogs.description: An easy‑to‑read explainer of the core idea behind BitNet b1.58: turning every weight into a ternary value (‑1, 0, +1). We'll walk through the quantization trick, why adding the zero value boosts performance, and how this tiny representation still matches full‑precision models on perplexity and downstream tasks.

blogs.title: Speed, Size, and Power: The Real‑World Gains of 1‑Bit LLMs
blogs.description: A deep dive into the practical benefits reported in the paper—faster inference, lower GPU memory, and massive energy savings. We'll translate the reported 2.7× speed‑up and 71× reduction in arithmetic energy into everyday terms for developers and data‑center operators.

blogs.title: Scaling Laws for 1.58‑Bit Models: Why Bigger Isn’t Always Better… Until It Is
blogs.description: An accessible overview of the new scaling law introduced by the authors, showing how a 13B BitNet b1.58 can outperform a 3B FP16 LLM in latency, memory, and energy. We'll illustrate the equivalence chart and discuss what this means for future model sizing decisions.

blogs.title: Building Edge‑Ready AI: Deploying 1‑Bit LLMs on Mobile and IoT Devices
blogs.description: Explores how the tiny weight size and 8‑bit activations open the door for running sophisticated language models on phones, tablets, and edge hardware. Includes a quick guide to what hardware changes (or lack thereof) are needed to make it happen.

blogs.title: Designing Tomorrow’s Chips for 1‑Bit LLMs
blogs.description: Looks ahead at hardware implications—from integer‑only matrix multiply units to new memory hierarchies—required to fully exploit BitNet’s computation paradigm. We'll compare existing designs like Groq’s LPUs with speculative architectures tailored for ternary weights.

blogs.title: Beyond Quantization: Training LLMs from Scratch with Ternary Weights
blogs.description: A tutorial‑style post that breaks down the training pipeline used for BitNet b1.58: the absmean quantizer, BitLinear layer, and integration with LLaMA‑style components. Ideal for researchers who want to experiment with low‑bit training on their own datasets.
